candidate.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: implement measures to prevent healthcare-associated infection and maintain clients receiving invasive respiratory support safely.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — VAP prevention and positioning
candidate.educational_objective: For mechanically ventilated adults without a contraindication, use 30–45-degree head-of-bed elevation as one component of VAP-prevention care while avoiding unsupported claims that this intervention alone reduces mortality or duration of ventilation.

options.A: Maintain head-of-bed elevation at approximately 30–45 degrees as an essential prevention practice.
options.B: Keep the client routinely supine because head-of-bed elevation has been shown to increase VAP rates.
options.C: Elevate the head of the bed only after VAP is diagnosed because positioning is a treatment rather than a prevention measure.
options.D: Use head-of-bed elevation as a substitute for other ventilator-prevention practices because it has been proven to reduce mortality and ventilation duration by itself.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. The current SHEA/IDSA/APIC acute-care prevention guidance lists head-of-bed elevation to 30–45 degrees as an essential practice for mechanically ventilated adults. The supporting meta-analysis found an association with lower VAP rates, but evidence quality was low and the guidance notes no demonstrated difference in duration of mechanical ventilation or mortality. B and C contradict the prevention recommendation. D overstates the evidence and incorrectly treats one prevention measure as a replacement for a broader ventilator-safety strategy.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Head-of-bed elevation to 30–45 degrees is an essential VAP/VAE prevention practice for mechanically ventilated adults, with evidence suggesting lower VAP rates but not proven mortality or ventilation-duration benefit.
